SOURCE: Generative Representational Instruction Tuning (GRIT / GritLM). Niklas Muennighoff, Hongjin Su, Liang Wang, Nan Yang, Furu Wei, Tao Yu, Amanpreet Singh, Douwe Kiela (Contextual AI, HKU, Microsoft). arXiv:2402.09906v3 [cs.CL], 3 Mar 2025. The text names no venue, so treat it as a preprint. v1 was Feb 2024. v2 (2024-04) added KTO. v3 (2025-03) added Appendix D and the intermediate-layer embedding discussion.

COVERAGE: 182,973 chars extracted. I read the main text (about 0-64,000 chars) in full. I also read Appendices A-G (ablation tables), D (extra RAG), H, L, M, Q, R and S. I skimmed or skipped the reference list, the dataset samples and the prompt appendices (O, P, J, K, N, I), which are templates. Extraction was clean. Full text is at /tmp/gritlm.txt.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- Unifying embedding and generation in one model costs nothing: GritLM 7B matches the embedding-only and generative-only variants.
  number: MTEB avg 66.8 for GritLM 7B vs 66.8 emb-only; generative avg 55.5 vs 55.2 gen-only.
  setup: Mistral 7B fine-tuned on E5S embedding data and Tülu 2 generative data. Same number of steps (1253). MTEB 56 datasets. Generative avg over MMLU, GSM8K, BBH, TyDi QA, HumanEval and AlpacaEval.
  quote: "GRIT LM 7B 79.5 50.6 87.2 60.5 57.4 83.4 30.4 66.8" and "Emb.-only 7B 78.8 51.1 87.1 60.7 57.5 83.8 30.2 66.8"
  where: Table 1, p5; Table 2, p5; text p6 ("GRIT LM matches embedding-only and generative-only variants")

- GritLM 7B set the MTEB state of the art among open models.
  number: MTEB avg 66.8, vs E5 Mistral 7B 66.6, BGE Large 0.34B 64.2, OpenAI v3 (proprietary) 64.6, Llama 2 70B 35.6 (weighted-mean pooling, not embedding-tuned).
  setup: 56 MTEB datasets. Retrieval nDCG 57.4 (vs E5-Mistral 56.9, OpenAI v3 55.4). GritLM 8x7B gets 65.7 because its embedding batch size was 256 instead of 2048 (compute limits).
  quote: "We find thatGRIT LM 7B outperforms all prior open models on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark [109] while still outperforming all generative models up to its size of 7 billion parameters."
  where: Table 1 and section 3.2, p5-6

- Training only one objective loses the other capability. Gen-only scores 41.2 on MTEB. The emb-only model and SGPT BE 5.8B score around random on generation (MMLU 23.5 and 24.4; random is 25.0).
  quote: "benchmarking the embedding performance of the generative-only model only leads to a score of 41.2 in Table 1. Thus, joint optimization via the GRIT approach is critical to achieve strong performance for both embedding and generation."
  where: p6

- RAG speedup from caching (the headline number): more than 60% faster RAG for long documents, because retriever and reader are the same model.
  number: Doc Caching, Sample A (4000-token doc, 1-token query), document-then-query prompt, CPU latency 14.18 s (RAG) to 5.25 s. That is 63% on CPU and 31% on GPU (0.39 s to 0.27 s). Query Caching, Sample B (4000-token query, 1-token doc): 54% on CPU, 33% on GPU.
  setup: GritLM 7B, Natural Questions, 2,681,468-doc BEIR NQ index. 16 generated tokens. Intel Xeon 8481C CPU and one H100 80GB. 100 runs. The RAG baseline uses the same 7B model for both retrieval and generation, without caching. Speedup is negligible at 250 cached tokens and grows with length. GPU gains are smaller because GPUs process the whole sequence in parallel.
  quote: "In Table 7, we display that for 4000 tokens, Query Caching is 54% and 33% faster on CPUs and GPUs, respectively (Sample B). For Doc Caching it is 63% and 31% (Sample A)."
  where: p14 (section 4 Latency); Table 7, p12; Fig 5, p13. The abstract's ">60%" is the CPU figure only.

- The paper does not give the pipeline pass count in Table 7. The intro states it: traditional RAG needs four forward passes (query and context through both models), and one model lets you cache and halve that.
  quote: "This requires passing the user query and the context into both the generative and the embedding model for a total of four forward passes. With GRIT LM, the embedding and generative model are equivalent, allowing us to cache computations and halve the necessary number of forward passes."
  where: p2-3

- Four caching variants.
  - Query Caching: reuse the key-value states from the query's embedding pass for the generative pass.
  - Doc Caching: store each document's key-value states in the index.
  - Query-Doc and Doc-Query Caching: cache both.
  - Doc Caching also works for non-GRIT models but needs every document passed through the generator when the index is built.
  quote: "Thus, the index consists of the document embeddings and key-value states." and "Doc Caching also works for models other than GRIT LM."
  where: p11

- Answer quality across caching variants (Natural Questions "match", 0-shot, GritLM 7B):

| Variant | Match |
|---|---|
| No RAG | 21.00 |
| RAG | 30.50 (30.47 for document-first) |
| Query Caching | 25.46 |
| Doc Caching | 33.38 (best) |
| Query-Doc Caching | 21.63 |
| Doc-Query Caching | 18.39 |

  - Query-Doc and Doc-Query Caching land near the No-RAG baseline.
  - Causes the authors give: bidirectional-attention mismatch and embedding-format mismatch.
  - They suggest a RAG finetuning stage would fix this (not done).
  - Doc Caching also matched or beat RAG on TriviaQA (57.93 vs 52.12) and MMLU (53.46 vs 51.10), Table 10.
  quote: "Meanwhile, Doc Caching slightly improves performance resulting in the best match score among all methods considered."
  where: Table 7 p12; p13-14; App. D

- Doc Caching trades latency for storage.
  number: about 30TB of key-value states for 2.68M documents, against 43GB for the index plus passages. About 12.5MB loaded per sample. The index is float32 and the key-value states are bfloat16. The key-value states can be offloaded to disk.
  quote: "this leads to around 30TB of key-value states."
  where: Table 7 and the Storage paragraph, p14

- Guidance on when to use which mode: Doc Caching for long documents, Query Caching for long queries. In production, "a simple input length check could switch from one caching mode to the other."
  where: p14

- Small embedding models gave much worse RAG answers with the same GritLM 7B generator.
  number: NQ match 10.39 (BGE Large 0.34B), 10.31 (BGE Base), 10.17 (BGE Small), vs 30.50 for GritLM RAG.
  setup: Table 7 setup, "Query then document" prompt. The authors attribute this to irrelevant passages confusing the generator.
  where: Table 11, App. D, p32

- Reranking with the same model: GritLM 7B, reranking its own top 10 via generative permutation generation (Sun et al. prompt), lifts the 15-dataset MTEB retrieval avg from 57.4 to 57.9. It improved 14 of 15 datasets (QuoraRetrieval dropped, 89.47 to 88.67). The conclusion says "15 out of 16 retrieval datasets" while Table 3 lists 15 datasets, a mismatch in the paper.
  quote: "Average 57.4 57.9"
  where: Table 3, p6

- Few-shot examples in embedding prompts do not help.
  quote: "We find that providing few-shot examples overall worsens performance."
  where: Table 4, p7 (for example ArguAna 63.2 to 51.7 with E5S)

- Embedding ablations (MTEB avg):
  - Bidirectional attention plus mean pooling beats causal. Unified: 64.0 vs 62.8 (Wmean) and 61.2 (last token).
  - Pre-finetuning embedding quality does not predict post-finetuning quality: GPT-J beats Mistral at raw embedding, but Mistral wins after finetuning.
  - Embedding data matters most: E5 66.0, MEDI2 64.7, MEDI 64.0.
  - Embedding batch size 4096 vs 256 gives +1.0 (64.2 vs 63.2).
  - Down-projecting 4096 to 1024 dims loses about 1% (62.7 to 62.1).
  - BF16 mixed precision matches FP32 (66.5 vs 66.3), as long as pooling and similarity stay in FP32.
  - Same-dataset in-batch negatives give +1.3 on retrieval (56.2 vs 54.9) but the same average.
  - Training with 2048 max document tokens beats 512: 64.7 vs 64.1.
  where: Table 6 p9, Tables 15-25

- Generative loss: mixing token-level and sample-level loss works best. Token-level loss across only 4 samples costs 7 AlpacaEval points (67.6 vs 74.7) and shortens generations (median length 941 to 865).
  where: Table 6k and p11

- KTO alignment after GRIT: AlpacaEval rises by more than 10 points. MTEB drops slightly (66.8 to 66.7; 65.7 to 65.2), because no embedding training happens in that stage.
  where: Table 5, p7

- Scale: GritLM 8x7B is the best open generative model on the paper's average (65.7; Tülu 2 70B 65.1; Mixtral 8x7B Instruct 60.3), using 13B parameters at inference. GritLM 7B generative avg is 55.5 vs Llama 2 70B 46.4.
  where: Table 2

- Training compute: GritLM 7B took 3,072 H100/A100 GPU hours (8 nodes x 8 A100 for 48 h). GritLM 8x7B took 20,480 GPU hours. Gen-only took 72 GPU hours and emb-only 1,760. About 100,000 GPU hours in total, including ablations.
  quote: "Adding up all ablations and evaluations, we likely used somewhere around 100,000 GPU hours."
  where: App. Q, p66. This shows the unified model is not cheaper to fine-tune.

LIMITS
- Costs the authors concede:
  - GRIT needs more finetuning compute than generative-only tuning, because it trains on two objectives.
  - GritLM 7B is far costlier to run than BGE Large (0.335B parameters).
  - Its embeddings are 4096-dim, 4x the storage of BGE's 1024-dim.
- Doc Caching needs about 30TB of key-value storage for a 2.7M-document corpus. The index is small, not web scale.
- The caching experiments use a single dataset (NQ) with a 2.68M-doc index. TriviaQA and MMLU were run on Doc Caching only. There are no real-world long-document benchmarks. Samples A and B are synthetic extremes (4000 tokens vs 1 token).
- The RAG baseline uses the 7B model for both stages. Production setups often use a much smaller embedder, and the authors only argue it would still be slower.
- Query Caching and Query-Doc caching lose accuracy. The authors say the problem is bidirectional vs causal key-value states, and the proposed fix (RAG finetuning on top of GritLM) is left to future work. Not using bidirectional attention would fix the mismatch but lowers embedding quality.
- The match metric is lenient (generous substring matching). Exact match gave 4 false negatives in the first 20 "No RAG" samples.
- Embeddings for inputs longer than 512 tokens are untested (no benchmark). The authors say they "do not know how well" these perform.
- They conceded that GritLM may have been tuned near the generative eval sets (Tülu 2 setup).
- Few-shot embedding does not work.
- Multilinguality and multimodality are untested. The agent self-retrieval idea is future work.
- The format wastes tokens: 13-15 tokens of framing.
- Dated: the comparisons are from Feb-Mar 2024 (Mistral/Mixtral, E5-Mistral, OpenAI v3, Llama 2, Zephyr). MTEB leaderboard rankings have since moved. The v3 text was not updated with later models, so I did not check anything newer.
- MT-Bench was dropped as unreliable: changing the judge from GPT-4 to GPT-4 Turbo cut avg scores 26% (3.36 to 2.48).

BUILDS ON
- Prior work this paper credits for its method:
  - SGPT (Muennighoff 2022): LLM embeddings, with a small change (BitFit) switching between embedding and generation.
  - Instructor / MEDI (Su et al. 2022): instruction-tuned embeddings.
  - E5 (Wang et al. 2022/2024): the embedding data.
  - Task-aware Retrieval with Instructions (Asai et al. 2022).
  - Tülu 2 (Ivison et al. 2023): the generative data and evaluation setup.
  - Mistral 7B and Mixtral (the base models).
  - Contrastive in-batch negatives (Chen et al. 2020, SimCLR).
  - KTO (Ethayarajh et al.).
  - CoCa (Yu et al. 2022): the unified visual model.
  - Sun et al. 2023: permutation-generation reranking.
  - Izacard et al. (Atlas): the RAG implementation, adapted.
  - Lin et al.: joint retriever/reader optimization (RA-DIT).
  - MTEB (Muennighoff et al. 2022).

CODE
- Loss (Eq. 1-3, p3-4): contrastive InfoNCE with in-batch negatives over mean-pooled, bidirectional hidden states, and next-token loss on the response tokens only.
  - L_GRIT = λ_Rep·L_Rep + λ_Gen·L_Gen.
- Format (Fig 3, p3): generation is "<s><|user|>\n{instruction}\n<|assistant|>\n{response}</s>". Embedding is "<s><|user|>\n{instruction}\n<|embed|>\n{sample}". Pool the final hidden states of the sample tokens only.
- Appendix H, Listing 1 (p40): splits the embedding triplet (q, p, n) into separate forward and backward passes to save memory.
- Repo: https://github.com/ContextualAI/gritlm. Models are on hf.co/GritLM.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): GritLM 7B and 8x7B sit top-right on an embedding-vs-generation scatter, a quick view of "best at both".
- Fig 2 (p2): one model, instruction chooses embedding or generation.
- Fig 3 (p3): architecture and format (bidirectional + mean pooling vs causal + LM head).
- Fig 4 (p12): the RAG caching diagram (Traditional RAG, Query Caching, Query-Doc Caching). This is the one to use in the RAG note.
- Fig 5 (p13): latency vs query/document length (250 to 4000 tokens) on CPU and GPU. It shows the speedup only appears for long inputs.
- I did not run the captions script; these captions come from the extracted text.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- The Fig 4 and Fig 5 extractions are garbled axis text. Table 7 values are clean.
- I read the figure-based appendix material (loss curves, prompt appendices O and P, hyperparameter appendix I) only by skimming, so I report no numbers from them.
- Internal inconsistency: the conclusion says reranking improves "15 out of 16 retrieval datasets", while Table 3 shows 15 datasets and 14 improved. The conclusion also says Doc Caching gives ">60%" at "no performance loss"; that holds only for the CPU figure on NQ.
- The "Doc-Query Caching" sentence says 54% for Query Caching (Sample B) and 63% for Doc Caching (Sample A). I confirmed the 63% from Table 7: 14.18 to 5.25 s.
